{{Short description|Function for Heun's differential equation}}
{{more footnotes|date=June 2017}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''local Heun function''' <math> H \ell (a,q;\alpha ,\beta, \gamma, \delta ; z)</math><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Heun |first=Karl |date=June 1888 |title=Zur Theorie der Riemann'schen Functionen zweiter Ordnung mit vier Verzweigungspunkten |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1428220 |journal=Mathematische Annalen |language=de |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=161–179 |doi=10.1007/BF01443849 |issn=0025-5831}}</ref> is the solution of '''Heun's differential equation''' that is holomorphic and 1 at the singular point ''z''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0. The local Heun function is called a '''Heun function''', denoted ''Hf'', if it is also regular at ''z''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, and is called  a '''Heun polynomial''', denoted ''Hp'',  if it is regular at all three finite singular points&nbsp;''z''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;''a''.

It is named after German mathematician [[Karl Heun]].

==Heun's equation==

Heun's equation is a second-order [[linear function|linear]] [[ordinary differential equation]] (ODE) of the form

:<math>\frac {d^2w}{dz^2} + 
\left[\frac{\gamma}{z}+ \frac{\delta}{z-1} + \frac{\epsilon}{z-a} \right] 
\frac {dw}{dz} 
+ \frac {\alpha \beta z -q} {z(z-1)(z-a)} w = 0.</math>

The condition <math>\epsilon=\alpha+\beta-\gamma-\delta+1</math> is taken so that the characteristic exponents for the regular singularity at infinity are α and β (see below).

The complex number ''q'' is called the '''accessory parameter'''. Heun's equation has four [[regular singular point]]s: 0,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;''a'' and ∞ with exponents (0,&nbsp;1&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;γ), (0,&nbsp;1&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;δ), (0,&nbsp;1&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;ϵ), and (α,&nbsp;β). Every second-order linear ODE on the extended complex plane with at most four regular singular points, such as the [[Lamé equation]] or the [[hypergeometric differential equation]], can be transformed into this equation by a change of variable.

Coalescence of various regular singularities of the Heun equation into irregular singularities give rise to several confluent forms of the equation, as shown in the table below.

:{| class="wikitable" 
|+Forms of the Heun Equation<ref>{{Cite web |title=DLMF: §31.12 Confluent Forms of Heun’s Equation ‣ Properties ‣ Chapter 31 Heun Functions |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/31.12 |access-date=2026-01-25 |website=dlmf.nist.gov}}</ref>
|-
! Form !! Singularities !! Equation
|-
| General
| 0, 1, ''a'', ∞
| <math>\frac{d^2w}{dz^2} + \left[\frac{\gamma}{z}+ \frac{\delta}{z-1} + \frac{\epsilon}{z-a} \right] \frac{dw}{dz} + \frac{\alpha \beta z -q}{z(z-1)(z-a)} w = 0</math>
|-
| Confluent
| 0, 1, ∞ (irregular, rank 1)
| <math>\frac{d^2w}{dz^2} + \left[\frac{\gamma}{z}+ \frac{\delta}{z-1} + \epsilon \right] \frac{dw}{dz} + \frac{\alpha z -q}{z(z-1)} w = 0</math>
|-
| Doubly Confluent
| 0 (irregular, rank 1), ∞ (irregular, rank 1)
| <math>\frac{d^2w}{dz^2} + \left[\frac{\delta}{z^2}+ \frac{\gamma}{z} + 1 \right] \frac{dw}{dz} + \frac{\alpha z -q}{z^2} w = 0</math>
|-
| Biconfluent
| 0, ∞ (irregular, rank 2)
| <math>\frac{d^2w}{dz^2} - \left[\frac{\gamma}{z}+ \delta + z \right] \frac{dw}{dz} + \frac{\alpha z -q}{z} w = 0</math>
|-
| Triconfluent
| ∞ (irregular, rank 3)
| <math>\frac{d^2w}{dz^2} + \left(\gamma + z \right) z \frac{dw}{dz} + \left(\alpha z -q\right) w = 0</math>
|}

==q-analog==
The [[q-analog]] of Heun's equation has been discovered by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Wolfgang Hahn|last=Hahn|year=1971}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hahn |first=W. |date=1971 |title=On linear geometric difference equations with accessory parameters |journal=Funkcial. Ekvac |volume=14 |pages=73-78}}</ref> and studied by Takemura in 2017.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Takemura |first=Kouichi |date=2017 |title=Degenerations of Ruijsenaars–van Diejen operator and q-Painlevé equations |url=http://academic.oup.com/integrablesystems/article/doi/10.1093/integr/xyx008/4159873/Degenerations-of-Ruijsenaarsvan-Diejen-operator |journal=Journal of Integrable Systems |language=en |volume=2 |issue=1 |arxiv=1608.07265 |doi=10.1093/integr/xyx008 |issn=2058-5985}}</ref>

==Symmetries==

Heun's equation has a group of symmetries of order 192, isomorphic to the [[Coxeter group]] of the [[Coxeter diagram]] ''D''<sub>4</sub>, analogous to the 24 symmetries of the [[hypergeometric differential equations]] obtained by Kummer.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}}

The symmetries fixing the local Heun function form a group of order 24 isomorphic to the [[symmetric group]] on 4 points, so there are 192/24 =&nbsp;8 =&nbsp;2&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;4 essentially different solutions given by acting on the local Heun function by these symmetries, which give solutions for each of the 2 exponents for each of the 4 singular points. The complete list of 192 symmetries was given by {{harvtxt|Maier|2007}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maier |first=Robert S. |date=2006-11-28 |title=The 192 solutions of the Heun equation |url=http://www.ams.org/mcom/2007-76-258/S0025-5718-06-01939-9/ |journal=Mathematics of Computation |language=en |volume=76 |issue=258 |pages=811–843 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-06-01939-9 |issn=0025-5718|arxiv=math/0408317 | ref = {{SfnRef|Maier|2007}} }}</ref> using machine calculation. Several previous attempts by various authors to list these by hand contained many errors and omissions;{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} for example, most of the 48 local solutions listed by Heun contain serious errors.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}}
